summary: Defines a part of the Management Information Base for hosts and routers that use a Multicast Address Resolution Server (MARS) for IP multicast over UNI 3.0/3.1 ATM networks. It was replaced by RFC 2417.

eli5.summary: A set of gauges for checking how group messages are handled on an ATM network.

subtitle: Management objects for IP multicast over ATM networks.

tldr.problem: ATM networks can carry IP multicast traffic, but network administrators needed a way to monitor and manage the MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) systems that handle multicast group address resolution.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2366 defines a collection of managed objects in the SNMP Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring MARS clients, MARS servers, and multicast servers on ATM networks, including their status, group memberships, and virtual circuits.
tldr.outcome: Administrators could monitor and manage IP multicast delivery over ATM networks, though ATM multicast support was eventually superseded by other technologies.

facts.label: Main components
facts.value: MARS Clients, Servers, and Multicast Servers

today: RFC 2366 was replaced by RFC 2417 in 1998. IP multicast over ATM networks saw limited adoption, and other technologies eventually became the dominant approach for multicast delivery.

sections.title: Management of Multicast on ATM
sections.content:
ATM networks can deliver group messages (IP multicast) to many endpoints at once. The MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) protocol, defined in RFC 2022, handles how these group memberships are tracked and distributed. RFC 2366 provides a Management Information Base (MIB) module so that network administrators using SNMP can monitor and manage MARS systems and related entities.

The MIB module defines managed objects for three types of systems: MARS clients (ATM-attached hosts and routers), MARS servers (the servers that distribute multicast information), and Multicast Servers (intermediate nodes that forward multicast traffic). The module is designed to be used with SNMPv2 and provides compatibility with SNMPv1.
sections.eli5: When a network sends messages to many computers at once (multicast), special servers (called MARS) help keep track of who wants the messages. This RFC is about the gauges and switches that let network managers see and control those servers.

sections.title: The Three MARS Roles
sections.content:
The MIB module defines objects for managing three distinct roles:

MARS Clients are ATM-attached hosts or routers that register with a MARS to join multicast groups. The client objects track the ATM address of the client, its registration status with the MARS, group memberships, backup MARS addresses, virtual circuits opened by the client, and statistics.

MARS Servers manage a cluster of clients and maintain information about multicast groups. Server objects track the MARS ATM address, the groups it serves, registered clients and multicast servers, virtual circuits it maintains, statistics, and mappings between groups and clients.

Multicast Servers (MCS) forward multicast traffic on behalf of clients. They register with a MARS and are tracked by their ATM address, registered groups, virtual circuits, and status.
sections.eli5: There are three types of boxes on an ATM network: clients (computers that want to receive group messages), MARS servers (that keep track of who wants what), and helper boxes (that actually forward the messages).

sections.title: The Managed Objects
sections.content:
Each role has multiple tables of managed objects. For clients, the MIB includes: a client table (address, MARS address, registration status, timers), a multicast group table (which groups the client joins), a backup MARS table (fallback MARS addresses), a virtual circuit table, and statistics. Key client attributes include the Host Sequence Number (HSN) for tracking membership, the Cluster Member Identifier (CMI) assigned by the MARS, and the default MTU (maximum transmission unit).

For MARS servers, the MIB tracks the main MARS table, multicast group assignments, registered clients and multicast servers, virtual circuit details, statistics, and two mapping tables: one for client-to-group mappings and one for multicast server-to-group mappings.

All tables support row management using SNMP: administrators can create, modify, and delete entries. Most objects are readable; many are writable, allowing administrators to configure timers, addresses, and group memberships.
sections.eli5: The MIB is like a filing cabinet with drawers for each thing the network manager needs to monitor: which clients are connected, which groups they joined, how well things are working, what went wrong.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The MIB includes many read-write and read-create objects that allow administrators to modify network configuration. Without proper security, unauthorized changes could disrupt multicast service. The RFC recommends using SNMPv3 with its User-based Security Model (USM, RFC 2274) and View-based Access Control Model (VACM, RFC 2275) to control who can modify MARS configuration objects.

Organizations should ensure that SNMP access to this MIB is restricted to administrators with legitimate rights to make changes. The RFC notes that read-only access may also need protection in some environments.
sections.eli5: Because network managers use SNMP to change settings, it is important to make sure only trusted people can access these controls, otherwise someone could break the multicast service.
